sub_questions.question_text: Please describe the clinical finding and mention possible diagnosis (30)
sub_questions.answer: Based on the finding of staphylococcus aureus (MRSA: positive), CRP Quantitative 20 mg/L, ESR 1 hour 85 mm/hr[cite: 14]. Osteolytic in both femoral and tibial implant surface, implant loosening[cite: 15]. The possible diagnosis is Prosthetic Joint Infection[cite: 15].

sub_questions.question_text: Explain the MSIS criteria! (40)
sub_questions.answer:
• Major criteria (diagnosis can be made when 1 major criteria exist)
  * sinus tract communicating with prosthesis
  * pathogen isolated by culture from 2 separate tissue/fluid samples from the affected joint
• Minor criteria (preoperative diagnosis)
  * the scores below are added together to determine:
  * ≥6 = infected; 2-5 = inconclusive; 0-1 = not infected - serum labs
  * elevated CRP (>10 mg/L) or D-dimer (>860 ng/mL) - 2 poin
  * elevated ESR (>30 mm/h) - 1 point - synovial fluid analysis
  * elevated synovial WBC (>3,000 cells/μl) or leukocyte esterase - 3 points
  * positive alpha-defensin - 3 points (most sensitive and specific marker for PJI)
  * elevated synovial PMN (>80%) - 2 points
  * elevated synovial CRP (>6.9 mg/L) - 1 point

sub_questions.question_text: Please describe about biofilm (30)
sub_questions.answer: A biofilm is an architectural colony of microorganisms, within a matrix of extracellular polymeric substance that they produce[cite: 27]. Biofilm contains microbial cells adherent to one another and to a static surface (living or non-living)[cite: 28]. Bacterial biofilms are usually pathogenic in nature and can cause nosocomial infections[cite: 29].

sub_questions.question_text: How do you classify this patology & please explain (20)
sub_questions.answer:
AVN of the left femoral head FICAT IV
Table 2 Ficat and arlet classification system
Stage 0: Normal radiographs (silent hip)
Stage 1: Slight abnormality as patchy/opaque areas, minor osteopenia
Stage II: Sclerotic or cystic lesions (II a: No crescent sign, Il b: Crescent sign without flattening of the femoral head)
Stage III: Flattening of the femoral head or femoral head collapse

sub_questions.question_text: Describe how to perform hand fasciotomy? what compartment release in each incision? (50)
sub_questions.answer:
Approach
  * Make two longitudinal incisions on 2nd and 4th metacarpals
  * To decompress volar/dorsal interossei and adductor compartment
  * Make longitudinal incision radial side of 1st metacarpal
  * To decompress thenar compartment
  * Make longitudinal incision over ulnar side of 5th metacarpal
  * To decompress hypothenar compartment
Technique
  * first volar interosseous and adductor pollicis muscles are decompressed through blunt dissection along ulnar side of 2nd metacarpal
Post-operative
  * wounds left open until primary closure is possible
  * if primary closure not possible, split-thickness skin grafting is used

sub_questions.question_text: Mention the prerequisites for tendon transfer surgery! (50)
sub_questions.answer:
Donor-related
  1. Adequate strength of the transferred tendon
  2. Synergism
  3. Expendable donor
  4. Amplitude of the transferred tendon should be as near to the original tendon for which the transfer is being done
Recipient-related
  1. Tissue should be in equilibrium
  2. Supple joints
  3. Try to restore sensibility of distal organ before treatment
  4. Arthrodesis/ joint procedure should be done before tendon transfer
  5. The disorder should be non progressive one
Technique-related
  1. One tendon, one function
  2. Straight line of pull
  3. Pass tendon below fascial plane
  4. Insertion of tendon should be as close to the insertion of paralyzed tendon
  * try to preserve nerve and vascular supply
  5. Keep dissection to minimum

sub_questions.question_text: According to Starr and Tsuge, mention the preferred combinations of tendon transfer for wrist, thumb, and fingers extension! (50)

FCR to EDC

sub_questions.question_text: Name 3 differential diagnoses that may produce such deformities. (25)

sub_questions.question_text: Please name the order of correction according to Ponseti? (25)
sub_questions.answer: Cavus, adductus, varus, equinus

sub_questions.question_text: Name 3 difference between Kite technique and Ponseti technique? (50)
sub_questions.answer:
1. Method of Manipulation
  Kite Technique: Focuses on correcting deformities one at a time, often starting with the forefoot adduction.
  Ponseti Technique: Corrects all deformities simultaneously, except equinus (which is corrected last), with a focus on abducting the foot while maintaining the talus as a fulcrum.
2. Fulcrum Point in Correction
  Kite Technique: Uses the calcaneocuboid joint as the fulcrum during manipulation.
  Ponseti Technique: Uses the head of the talus as the fulcrum for abducting the foot.
3. Success Rate and Popularity
  Kite Technique: Has a lower success rate and is largely considered outdated due to suboptimal outcomes and longer treatment durations.
  Ponseti Technique: Has a higher success rate, is faster, less invasive, and is now the gold standard globally for clubfoot treatment.

sub_questions.question_text: If the patient requires surgery, please explain briefly of the evaluation and preparation must be done to the patient?(30)
sub_questions.answer:
• History and clinical presentation: patient activity, menarch status, family history
• Physical examination Skin condition or cutaneous changes, Deformity, rib humb, pelvic tilt.
• Adam forward bending test and limb length measurement.
• Neurological Examination: motoric and sensoric evaluation, physiological and pathological reflexes, special tests to deternine any UMN or LMN pathology (if present)
• Radiographic Measurement: Cobb angle, Balance Assesment (C7 Plumb line), Vertebral rotation (Nashmoe Method), Skeletal maturity (Risser Sign)
• Inform Consent, Laboratorium test and implant preparation
• Rehabilitatiom after surgery

sub_questions.question_text: Please explain why the leg pain worsened when the patient standing & improves with bending forward!(30)
sub_questions.answer: Caused by thickening of flavum ligament. When the patient is in standing position/erect/extension position, there will be buckling of flavum ligament, causing decrease of spinal canal, compression of thecal sac and if progressive will lead to ischaemia. When the patient is in flexion position, flavum will be in tension, creating a relatively widened spinal canal.

sub_questions.question_text: Please explain about the prognostic factors of this case! (20)
sub_questions.answer:
Tumor stage: the most important prognostic indicator
Tumor size: larger tumors generally have a worse prognosis
Wide surgical margin: high risk of local recurrence with inadequate resection
Response to chemotherapy: correlating with a poor prognosis and a higher propensity for metastatic disease
ALP Level: pre-treatment ALP is associated with a high tumor burden and a worse prognosis
The presence of distant metastases

sub_questions.question_text: Please explain about the treatment plan in this case! (20)
sub_questions.answer:
Systemic control
  Pain management with WHO step ladder protocol
  Neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy
Local control
  Surgical management of osteosarcoma wide resection with negative margin

sub_questions.question_text: Please explain the resection classification!(20)
sub_questions.answer:
Intralesional Excision
  An excision performed within the tumor mass, involving partial removal or debulking. This procedure leaves macroscopic residual tumor tissue and the pseudocapsule in situ.
Marginal Excision
  A tumor dissection carried out through the reactive zone (pseudocapsule). This technique may result in microscopic residual disease.
Wide (En Bloc) Excision
  An excision performed to remove the entire tumor, the pseudocapsule, and a complete cuff of surrounding normal tissue. This is the recommended technique for sarcomas, although the requisite thickness of the normal tissue margin remains a matter of controversy For soft tissue and bone sarcomas, a margin of 0.5-2 cm is generally accepted. This technique may still leave residual tumor cells in the event of skip metastases.
Radical Excision
  An excision involving the removal of the entire tumor mass along with the whole of anatomical compartment from which it arises. This technique eliminates the possibility of leaving residual skip metastases.

sub_questions.question_text: Please explain about HUVOS grade!(20)
sub_questions.answer:
HUVOS grade is one of the pathological grading systems of tumor response to chemotherapy[cite: 401]. The Huvos grading system is divided into four tiers. Grades III and IV are characterized by extensive or complete tumor cell destruction, indicating necrosis greater than 90%. These grades are associated with a favorable prognosis and, consequently, better overall survival. Conversely, Grades I and II exhibit minimal tissue necrosis (less than 90%), correlating with a poor prognosis and a higher propensity for metastatic disease. The treatment plan is then adjusted based on this assessment: if the tumor demonstrates a good chemotherapeutic response (Huvos Grade III or IV), the current chemotherapy regimen is continued. However, if the response is poor (Huvos Grade I or II), the chemotherapy agents are typically modified or substituted.

Huvos grade | Percent necrosis (%) | Histologic effect
--- | --- | ---
I | 0-50 | Little or no effect identified
II | 51-90 | Areas of acellular tumor osteoid, necrotic, or fibrotic material attributable to the effect of chemotherapy, with other areas of histologically viable tumor
III | 91-99 | Predominant areas of acellular osteoid, necrotic, or fibrotic material attributable to the effect of chemotherapy, with only scattered foci of histologically viable tumor cells identified
IV | 100 | No histologic evidence of viable tumor identified within the entire specimen

sub_questions.answer: Intralesional Excision Extended Curretage + Bone Graft/Bone Cement

sub_questions.question_text: Explain about recurrence rate in this this patient!(20)
sub_questions.answer: Giant cell tumor has a high rate of recurrence of about 25-35%. Recurrence typically occurs within 3 years of curettage

sub_questions.question_text: Explain about metastase risk in this kind of case?(20)
sub_questions.answer: Although it is classified as benign tumor, the nature of giant cell tumor is an aggressive tumor, so it still has risk for metastasis, with the lungs being the most common site, affecting an estimated 1% to 5% of cases

sub_questions.question_text: Explain about possibility of malignancy in this case?(20)
sub_questions.answer: The risk of malignancy in a giant cell tumor (GCT) of bone is low, with an overall incidence reported to be between 1% and 2%. Malignant transformation is more likely to occur after multiple local recurrences or a GCT has been treated with radiation therapy, classifying it as a 'secondary' malignancy
